processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Each steel composition (including Al-10 / Fe30Mn10Al1C) first melted in a high-frequency vacuum induction furnace with a 50 kg capacity.
Cast into an ingot with a diameter of 150 mm.
Ingots homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h before hot rolling.
Hot rolled into rods with a diameter of 16 mm.
Hot-rolled rods air-cooled to room temperature.

processing_steps.method: solution treatment followed by water quenching
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot-rolled rods solution-treated at 1050 °C for 2 h followed by water quenching; this is the final state (proc_st-1050c-2h-wq) for the Al-10 sample used for tensile, Charpy impact and EBSD/TEM characterization.

structures.overall_structure: After solution treatment at 1050 °C for 2 h + water quenching the Fe30Mn10Al1C (Al-10) low-density steel consists of a single austenite (FCC) phase with a high fraction of annealing twin boundaries and uniformly distributed nano-scale κ-carbides (~1 nm); no ferrite (BCC) phase is present (f_Bcc = '-').

phases_present.morphology: equiaxed grains with numerous annealing twin boundaries

precipitates.distribution: uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix (intragranular)

interfaces.slip_behavior: κ-carbides are sheared by gliding dislocations (particle shear strengthening model) rather than being bypassed by an Orowan mechanism; shear deformation facilitates dislocation glide across κ-carbide shear planes, weakening the work-hardening rate. The shear strengthening contribution is described by σ_shear = α f^(1/2) d_Car^(1/2).
interfaces.phase_evolution: κ-carbides precipitate from spinodal decomposition and ordering of C and Al in the austenite; their size grows strongly with increasing C and Al content and decreases with increasing Mn content.
interfaces.interface_notes: Orientation relationship between κ-carbides and austenite: (001)κ || (001)γ; in coarse carbides growth was confined by the {011} growth plane, giving a rectangular shape.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: round tensile specimen, gauge length 25 mm, diameter 5 mm; tensile axis parallel to rod axis
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: tensile tests at an initial strain rate of 1.1×10^-3 s^-1 using an MTS tensile machine; two solution-treated specimens tested and data are the average of two specimens

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: Charpy V-notch specimen 55 mm × 10 × 10 mm with 2 mm deep V-notch; notch perpendicular to the rod axis

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: EBSD system on FEI Quanta 650 field emission gun SEM (Thermo Fisher Scientific); operating voltage 20 kV; step size 0.5 μm; Channel 5 post-processing software
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: specimens mechanically ground flat and electro-polished in 7% Nital at room temperature; grain size by linear intercept with 15° boundary definition
characterization_methods.purpose: determine phase distribution and average grain size as a function of alloying content
characterization_methods.key_findings: For the 10% Al steel a single austenite phase is present with no ferrite; average austenite grain size 29.7 ± 1.1 μm and twin boundary fraction f_Tw = 53.2%.

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: TEM Tecnai G2 F20 S-TWIN (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated at 200 kV
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: thin foils prepared by twin-jet electro-polishing in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol, at 20 V and -20 °C; dark-field images taken along [001]γ zone axis using a κ-carbide reflection
characterization_methods.key_findings: Extensive κ-carbide formation observed for Al contents of 10% and larger, with average κ-carbide diameter about 1 nm (Table 3: 1.0 ± 0.4 nm), uniformly distributed and coherent with the austenite matrix (orientation relationship (001)κ || (001)γ).

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: room temperature; initial strain rate 1.1×10^-3 s^-1; round specimen gauge length 25 mm, diameter 5 mm
characterization_methods.purpose: obtain stress-strain responses and strain hardening rates

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: -40 °C; V-notch perpendicular to the rod axis; specimen 55 mm × 10 × 10 mm with 2 mm V-notch

computational_details.simulation_method: analytical models (least-squares linear fitting and mechanistic equations)
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Linear fits of yield strength, tensile strength, elongation and area reduction against the square root of κ-carbide size gave good linear relationships (Fig. 7); density equation (Eq. 3) reproduced measured densities including that of Fe30Mn10Al1C.

analytical_models.model_note: σ_TS corresponds to the maximum true stress just before necking (crack nucleation).
σ_EF is the engineering fracture stress at sample breakage; A denotes maximum area reduction.
Linear least-squares fit of measured densities; for the Al-10 composition (C 1.01, Al 10.13, Mn 30.22 mass%) this yields ~6.6 g/cm3, matching the measured 6.69 g/cm3.
Shear model rather than Orowan; used because κ-carbides are coherent with the austenite matrix.
Linear fit of yield strength against the square root of the average κ-carbide size (Fig. 7a).
Linear fit of tensile strength against the square root of the average κ-carbide size (Fig. 7a).

unmapped_findings: Measured chemical composition of the Al-10 (Fe30Mn10Al1C) steel: C 1.01, Mn 30.22, Al 10.13, Fe Bal. (mass%), with measured density 6.69 g/cm3 (Table 1).

Inconsistency: the conclusions state the Fe30Mn10Al1C steel gives an excellent combination of yield strength 642 MPa, ductility 72% and impact toughness at -40 °C of 247 J at density 6.69 g/cm3, whereas Table 2 lists Akv-40 = 237 ± 5 J for the Al-10 steel (and the discussion text also lists Fe30Mn10Al1.0C as 237 J).
Only three of the designed low-density steels possessed high impact toughness, specifically Fe30Mn6Al1.0C (354 J), Fe30Mn8Al1.0C (294 J) and Fe30Mn10Al1.0C (237 J, Table 2).

No ferrite (BCC) phase is detected in the Al-10 steel (f_Bcc = '-'); a small ferrite volume fraction (3.08–3.1%) is observed only in the 12% Al steel. Ferrite refinement of austenite grain size is not strongly dependent on the ferrite volume fraction.

Effect of Al on work hardening (Fig. 8c): the work-hardening rate increases with decreasing Al content (maximum ~2100 MPa for the 6% Al steel), so the Al-10 steel has a lower work-hardening capacity than lower-Al steels; for all compositions σ_TS (~1350 MPa) and σ_FS (~2150 MPa) are nearly constant.

For Al contents of 8–11% only a single austenite phase is present after 1050 °C/2 h solution treatment + water quenching; extensive κ-carbide formation is observed for Al contents of 10% and larger, with average κ-carbide diameters of ~1 nm (10%Al), ~1.5 nm (11%Al) and ~15 nm (12%Al).
